meta.title: Ticket Booking
meta.summary: Sell seats for big events without double booking anyone, even when millions arrive at once, like Ticketmaster.

functional: Browse events and see which seats are available
Hold seats for a few minutes while paying
Release seats when a hold expires
nonFunctional: Never sell the same seat twice
99.95% availability for holding and paying during an on-sale
Holding a seat takes under 500 ms
Fair access when demand far exceeds seats

scale.label: Admitted
scale.value: ~2,000 fans/s from the waiting room, each a hold then a payment (~4,000 requests/s)

scale.label: Browsing
scale.value: ~100,000 page views/s at peak, mostly cached

scale.label: Bookings
scale.value: ~50M a year (~4.2M a month, ~140k a day)

nodes.label: WAF
nodes.description: Web ACL on the CDN: bot control, rate rules per IP and account, managed rule sets

nodes.label: CDN
nodes.description: Caches event pages and seat maps for a few seconds

nodes.label: Waiting Room
nodes.description: Gives each fan a signed place in line and admits them in order at a rate booking can take; its line counters live in the Seat Holds Redis

nodes.label: Internal Load Balancer
nodes.description: Private L7 load balancer in front of the Booking Service fleet, with health checks

nodes.label: Event Catalog
nodes.description: Events, venues and approximate seat availability

nodes.label: Booking Service
nodes.description: Holds seats, takes payment and confirms bookings

nodes.label: Seat Holds
nodes.description: One key per held seat with a 10-minute expiry; keys hash-tagged by event so a multi-seat hold is one atomic script

nodes.label: Bookings DB
nodes.description: Events, one row per seat (free or sold), bookings; a seat flips to sold only once

nodes.label: Ticket Queue
nodes.description: At-least-once delivery; a dead-letter queue after 5 failed attempts

nodes.label: Ticket Issuer
nodes.description: Creates signed barcodes (key in KMS) and emails tickets

flows.title: Browse an event
flows.summary: Reads are cheap and slightly stale; exact availability is checked only when holding.

steps.label: GET /events/123/seats
steps.detail: Every request, cached or not, passes the web ACL at the edge first.

steps.label: bot control + rate rules
steps.detail: Before an on-sale, bots hammer seat maps to find inventory. Bot control challenges scripted clients and rate rules cap requests per IP, so the CDN and origin only see people.

steps.label: cached for 5 s?
steps.detail: Seat maps are public and identical for every fan, so the cache key is the path alone (no cookies or auth headers). They are cached for 5 s; during an on-sale this absorbs almost all browsing, and a few seconds of staleness is fine because the hold re-checks every seat.

steps.label: cache miss: forward
steps.detail: An origin shield in front of the origin collapses misses from every edge location, so roughly one request per event every 5 s reaches the catalog.

steps.label: route to catalog
steps.detail: The public load balancer routes /events/* straight to the catalog; only hold and pay go through the waiting room.

steps.label: seat availability by section
steps.payload:
SELECT section, count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'free') AS free
FROM seats WHERE event_id = 123 GROUP BY section
steps.detail: Counts sold seats from the seat rows. Seats held in Redis still show as free here; the map is a guide, and the hold decides.

flows.title: Hold seats during an on-sale
flows.summary: The waiting room meters traffic; an atomic hold stops two fans taking the same seat.

steps.label: POST /holds (A12, A13)
steps.detail: The waiting room admitted this fan earlier and gave them a signed admission token, sent with every hold and pay request.

steps.label: bot control + rate rules
steps.detail: Holds are what scalpers' bots want. The web ACL challenges suspected bots and caps holds per IP before they reach the waiting room.

steps.label: allowed: forward
steps.detail: POST /holds is never cached: the CDN only terminates TLS near the fan and forwards to the origin.

steps.label: check admission token
steps.detail: Only fans the waiting room has admitted get through. It lets them in at a rate the booking service can take, in arrival order, instead of letting 5 million requests hit it at once.

steps.label: token valid: admitted
steps.detail: The token is signed by the room and bound to the fan's account, the event and an expiry, so checking it needs no lookup and it cannot be passed to another account.

steps.label: hold A12, A13 for fan u9
steps.detail: The room reaches the booking fleet through a private load balancer that health-checks every instance across the three zones. It starts the trace here.
steps.payload:
POST /internal/holds HTTP/1.1
traceparent: 00-0af7651916cd43dd8448eb211c80319c-b7ad6b7169203331-01
X-Fan-Id: u9
Idempotency-Key: 4c1e…

steps.label: hold A12 + A13 atomically, 10 min
steps.detail: One Lua script holds all the seats or none: two fans asking for overlapping seats can never each end up with half. The {123} hash tag puts an event's seat keys in one Redis slot so the script may touch them all, and a seat already held by u9 counts as success, so a retried request is harmless.
steps.payload:
EVALSHA hold_all 2 hold:{123}:A12 hold:{123}:A13 u9 600
-- for each key: if it exists and is not u9, return 0 (nothing set)
-- otherwise SET key u9 EX 600 for every key, return 1

steps.label: INSERT booking pending
steps.detail: The pending booking records which seats were held and when the hold expires, so payment and refunds can find it. Its expiry is taken from the same 10 minutes the Redis keys got.

flows.title: Pay and get tickets
flows.summary: Charge once, confirm only if the hold is still valid, then issue tickets in the background.

steps.label: still mine? extend 5 min
steps.detail: Before taking money, confirm the seats are still held by u9 and extend the hold so it cannot run out while the card is being charged.
steps.payload:
EVALSHA extend_all 2 hold:{123}:A12 hold:{123}:A13 u9 300
-- if every key still holds u9: EXPIRE each by 300 s, return 1; else return 0

steps.label: charge, key = b1-a1
steps.detail: The key is the booking plus the payment attempt: a retry after a timeout reuses it and cannot charge twice, while a fan who tries a different card after a decline gets a new attempt (b1-a2). The call leaves through the NAT gateway.

steps.label: confirm booking + flip seats to sold
steps.detail: One transaction: the booking must still be pending, and each seat row must still be free. Flipping a seat from free to sold can only happen once, so it is the final guard against a double sale, even if Redis lost a hold. If either check fails, the transaction rolls back and the charge is refunded (see the expiry flow).

steps.label: issue tickets for b1
steps.detail: Sent after the commit. If the service dies between the commit and the send, a background sweep in the booking service re-sends confirmed bookings not yet marked enqueued; that can send a booking twice, which the issuer tolerates.

steps.label: receive
steps.detail: Long-polls the queue. A message is deleted only after the email is accepted, so a crash means redelivery, and a message that fails 5 times moves to the dead-letter queue.

steps.label: sign barcodes
steps.detail: Each barcode is a signature over (event, seat, booking) with a key held in KMS, so the venue can check it offline. The same input always gives the same barcode, so a redelivered message re-sends identical tickets instead of minting new ones.

steps.label: send tickets
steps.detail: A duplicate email carries the same tickets, so it is harmless.

flows.title: Hold lost during payment: refund
flows.summary: The charge succeeds but a seat was sold to someone else (the hold expired or Redis lost it in a failover). The database refuses the second sale and the fan is refunded.

steps.label: charge, key = b7-a1
steps.detail: Booking b7 for seat C4 got through the hold check, but its Redis key was lost in a failover a moment later and another fan held and bought C4.

steps.label: confirm b7 + flip C4 to sold
steps.detail: The same transaction as a normal payment.
steps.payload:
UPDATE seats SET status = 'sold', booking_id = 'b7'
WHERE event_id = 123 AND seat = 'C4' AND status = 'free';  -- 0 rows: ROLLBACK

steps.label: 0 rows: seat already sold
steps.detail: The database is the referee: whatever Redis said, a seat row flips to sold once.

steps.label: refund, key = refund-b7-a1
steps.detail: The refund has its own idempotency key, so retrying it after a timeout cannot refund twice. The booking is marked refunded in the same step.

steps.label: Seat taken, you were refunded
steps.detail: Rare, because the hold is checked and extended just before charging. It is counted, since a rise means holds are being lost.

notes.text: Holding seats in Redis makes holds fast, atomic and self-cleaning. Redis replicates asynchronously, so a failover can lose recent holds and let two fans hold one seat; the seat row in the database still sells it only once, and the loser is refunded. If Redis is down entirely, holds stop (fail closed), because selling without a hold sends every admitted fan to the database at once.

The waiting room turns a spike of millions into a steady flow the booking service can handle, and gives fans a fair, visible place in line. It admits about 2,000 fans/s; six booking instances at about 1,000 requests/s each carry the resulting ~4,000/s, and still do with a zone lost.
Event pages and seat maps are cached for seconds at the CDN. Exact availability is only checked when a fan tries to hold a seat.

Each seat is one row that flips from free to sold once, inside the confirming transaction. That is the last line of defence against double booking, whatever happens upstream in Redis. Aurora keeps commits in three zones, so losing a zone costs a failover of about a minute but no confirmed sale.

Bots are the main threat to an on-sale. The web ACL on the CDN runs bot control, rate rules per IP and per account, and managed rule sets before the waiting room; admission tokens are signed and bound to one account; the barcode signing key never leaves KMS, so a stolen database dump cannot mint tickets.

slos.name: Hold and pay availability
slos.sli: Hold and pay requests from admitted fans answered without a 5xx, at the load balancer

slos.name: Fast holds
slos.sli: Hold requests answered within the threshold, measured at the booking service

slos.name: No seat sold twice
slos.sli: Seats with more than one issued ticket or confirmed booking, found by an audit query every 5 minutes; good means zero

alerts.when: Hold or pay errors burning the error budget 14 times too fast (checked over 5 minutes and 1 hour)
alerts.why: During an on-sale every minute of errors is lost sales and angry fans.

alerts.when: Hold or pay errors burning the error budget 3 times too fast (checked over 2 hours and 1 day)
alerts.why: A slow leak between on-sales, worth fixing before the next big one.

alerts.when: p99 hold latency above 500 ms for 5 minutes
alerts.why: Slow holds make fans retry, which multiplies the load at the worst moment.

alerts.when: The audit finds any seat with two confirmed bookings
alerts.why: A correctness bug that hurts real people at the venue door; stop sales for that event.

alerts.when: Oldest message in the Ticket Queue older than 10 minutes, or any message in its dead-letter queue
alerts.why: Paid fans are waiting for tickets; usually the issuer or the email provider is failing.

alerts.when: Payment provider timeouts and 5xx above 2% of charges for 15 minutes
alerts.why: A cause worth chasing before it becomes an SLO burn.

alerts.when: More than 0.1% of successful charges refunded because the seat was gone, over 15 minutes
alerts.why: Holds are being lost (Redis failover or memory pressure) or the hold check before charging is broken.

alerts.when: Seat Holds memory above 80%, any evicted keys, or a failover
alerts.why: An evicted or lost hold lets a second fan take the seat; the database still prevents the double sale, but fans get refunds.

signals.name: Active holds
signals.why: Seats currently held; compare with seats left to see how close an event is to selling out.

signals.name: Fans waiting
signals.why: The queue length and admission rate tell fans how long they will wait.

signals.name: Hold conflicts
signals.why: Fans trying to hold seats someone else holds; high during an on-sale, but a spike at quiet times points at stale seat maps.

signals.name: Seats sold against remaining
signals.why: The business view of an on-sale: when the event will sell out and whether to stop admitting fans.

signals.name: Refunds because the seat was gone
signals.why: Each one is a fan who paid and lost the seat; should be close to zero.

signals.name: Blocked requests by rule
signals.why: Bot traffic peaks just before an on-sale opens; a sudden drop in blocks can mean bots got past the rules.

debug.symptom: Fans keep seeing 'seat no longer available'
steps: Check hold conflicts: is it real demand or stale seat maps?
Check the CDN cache time on seat maps; too long shows taken seats as free.
Check how many seats sit in holds from fans who never pay: on a hot event a shorter hold returns seats sooner.
Check Seat Holds for evictions or a recent failover, which make holds disappear and show up as refunds.

debug.symptom: Payments succeed but no tickets arrive
steps: Check the age of the oldest message in the Ticket Queue.
Look at Ticket Issuer errors and retries in its logs.
Check the email provider's bounce and throttling dashboards.
Find one booking id and follow its trace from confirm to email.

questions.q: Two fans click the same seat at the same moment. How do you guarantee only one gets it?
questions.a: Make the hold an atomic all-or-nothing script over the seats' keys, so only one fan gets each seat and the other is told it is taken. Confirmation then flips each seat row from free to sold inside one transaction, which can only succeed once per seat even if Redis lost a hold. No read-then-write in two steps anywhere.

questions.q: Five million fans arrive for 50,000 seats. What stops the system from falling over?
questions.a: A virtual waiting room in front of booking admits fans in arrival order at a rate the booking service and database can sustain, and shows everyone their place in line. Browsing is served from the CDN. Without it, retries from frustrated fans multiply the load and nobody gets through.

questions.q: How do abandoned holds get released, and what if the expiry fires while the fan is paying?
questions.a: Holds expire on their own after ten minutes, so abandoned seats return to sale without a cleanup job. Just before charging, the booking service checks the hold is still the fan's and extends it, so expiry during payment is rare; if a seat was lost anyway, the database refuses the sale and the charge is refunded with its own idempotency key.

questions.q: The payment provider times out. Was the fan charged?
questions.a: You do not know, so never charge with a new key. Retry with the same attempt key, or ask the provider for the payment status, and keep the booking pending with its hold extended meanwhile. A background job in the booking service settles anything still unclear, refunding if the seats are gone.

questions.q: One event's seat rows become a hot spot in the database. How do you spread the load?
questions.a: Keep contention in the hold store, which is in memory and handles per-seat keys well, and write to the database only for pending and confirmed bookings. Partition seats by event and section so one event does not lock a whole table, and keep transactions short.

questions.q: How do you stop bots from buying all the tickets?
questions.a: Layer the defences: bot control and per-IP rate rules at the WAF, verified accounts, admission tokens bound to one account, per-account and per-card limits, and randomising order among fans who arrive before the sale opens. Monitoring purchase patterns lets you cancel obvious bot bookings later.
